deep.reconstruction:
There are no computations or derivations on this page. It holds three separate notebook entries.

(A) The end of a remark that starts on the previous page. Weierstrass is called 'the Euclid of analysis' because he set out the foundations and assumptions strictly and built analysis consistently on them. Those assumptions are 'nothing other than calculating with whole positive integers, which intuition (Anschauung) teaches'. Hilbert refers to Kant, who presents these facts as a priori, and says one cannot reduce them further. Hence the assertions of mathematics are exactly as certain as calculation with whole numbers.

This is the 'arithmetization of analysis' standpoint (Weierstrass, Kronecker, Dedekind), given a Kantian epistemological grounding. Formally it says that analysis is conservatively reducible to arithmetic of the natural numbers N, and that certainty transfers along that reduction.

(B) Two proposed hydrodynamic (aerodynamic) problems.
(1) A horizontal plate (Wand) falls under gravity, first in still air and then in slightly moving air (wind). Experiments reportedly show a large difference, and Hilbert wants this shown theoretically. In modern terms: the drag on a horizontal plate falling normally in still air, compared with the force on the plate when a horizontal relative wind is present. With wind, the plate acts as a wing at small angle of attack and gains lift, so it falls far more slowly. This is the phenomenon emphasized by Lilienthal (1889) and Langley (1891).
(2) A hollow vessel, i.e. an umbrella (Schirm), receives roughly the same pressure whether the wind strikes it obliquely or head-on. For a flat plate, by contrast, the 'sine curve' holds: the normal pressure is proportional to sin(alpha), where alpha is the inclination to the wind. This is the empirical sine law, as opposed to Newton's theoretical sin^2 law.
The closest available theory at the time is Kirchhoff (1869) and Rayleigh (1876) free-streamline flow. It gives the normal force on an inclined flat plate as N(alpha) proportional to pi*sin(alpha)/(4+pi*sin(alpha)), so N(alpha)/N(pi/2) = (4+pi)*sin(alpha)/(4+pi*sin(alpha)). (This connection is my addition, not on the page.) No solution is attempted on the page.

(C) The start of an anecdote, continued on the next page. Hilbert plans to tell Gordan: 'When you come, I know either: it is Prof. Gordan, or it is not Prof. Gordan.' Gordan, Hilbert says, would add 'or thirdly, the person coming is neither.' This is a joke about the law of excluded middle (tertium non datur). It links to Gordan's objection to Hilbert's non-constructive existence proof of the finite basis theorem (1888/1890).
errors: No mathematical errors, since there are no derivations.

The claim about the flat plate is empirical, not exact. The 'sine law' (pressure proportional to sin alpha) was an empirical rule of thumb. Newton's impact theory gives sin^2(alpha). Kirchhoff–Rayleigh free-streamline theory gives (4+pi)sin(alpha)/(4+pi sin(alpha)), which exceeds sin(alpha) at small angles.
The umbrella claim is also only experimental. The pressure on a concave body is not exactly independent of angle; the note says 'ziemlich' (roughly).

results.what: Mathematics (via Weierstrass's rigorous foundations of analysis) rests ultimately on arithmetic of positive integers, which is known a priori through intuition in Kant's sense; hence mathematical assertions are as certain as integer arithmetic.
results.modern_name: Arithmetization of analysis; Kantian intuition as the basis of arithmetic
results.usually_credited_to: Weierstrass, Kronecker, Dedekind (arithmetization, 1860s–1880s); Kant (a priori intuition)

deep.surprise_reason: Hilbert's early Kantian and arithmetizing view of foundations is well documented, and so is his interest in physics. The Gordan excluded-middle joke fits the well-known basis-theorem controversy, and entries from these notebooks have been quoted by historians (e.g. Rowe, Corry). The hydrodynamic problems are only posed, not solved, and reflect the aeronautics discussion of around 1890. At most this is a minor biographical detail.

checkable.asserts: The Rayleigh free-streamline normal-force ratio equals 1 for normal incidence.
At small angles the Rayleigh formula exceeds the pure sine law by the factor (4+pi)/4 (about 1.785).
Newton's sin^2 law is much smaller than the sine law at small angles, which is why the empirical 'sine curve' contradicted Newton's theory.
Kirchhoff's normal-plate drag coefficient factor pi/(4+pi) (about 0.44 of stagnation pressure times area).

transcription_corrections: 'Holzgefäss' is very probably 'Hohlgefäss' (hollow vessel), which fits 'd. h. Schirm' (i.e. umbrella).
The inserted 'erhält ziemlich' belongs after 'Schirm', marked by the caret: 'Hohlgefäss d. h. Schirm erhält ziemlich den gleichen Druck'.
'kommen' is written 'komen' with a nasal stroke ('Wenn Sie komen'), meaning 'kommen'.
'Sinuscurve' is written 'Sinuscurve' (or 'Sinuscurve gilt'), which agrees with the transcription.
